part_title: AWS Console, Security Responsibilities and Safe Learning Costs
review_basis: Visually inspected AIF M02 original slides 26–29: global versus regional console services, shared responsibility, AWS Acceptable Use Policy and budgeting; explicitly clarify Rekognition classification and alerts not being spending caps.

scenes.title: Finding services in the AWS Console
scenes.narration: The AWS Management Console is a web interface where authorized people can discover and manage AWS services. This slide separates services that behave globally from those that operate within a selected Region. First look left. AWS Identity and Access Management, often called IAM, helps control who can do what in an AWS account. Amazon Route 53 helps manage DNS, CloudFront delivers supported content through edge locations, and AWS Organizations helps manage multiple accounts. These are examples with global aspects, although specific service configurations and related resources can still have regional details. Now look at the center: Amazon EC2, Elastic Beanstalk, AWS Lambda and Amazon Rekognition are shown as services that commonly use regional resources. Lambda runs code in response to events, and Rekognition analyzes images or videos using supported AI capabilities. The example on the right shows searching for IAM versus searching for EC2. The console may let you open IAM without choosing a regional workload, whereas creating an EC2 virtual machine requires an appropriate Region selection. Before launching any resource, confirm the Region shown in the console so you don't accidentally look in one Region for a resource created in another. The diagram classifies Rekognition as SaaS, but AWS Rekognition is more precisely a managed AI service and API, not an ordinary finished productivity application like hosted email. Likewise, not every service can be understood through one rigid global-or-regional label. The bottom note gives AWS WAF as an example: its configuration scope depends on whether it protects a regional resource or CloudFront. A useful beginner habit is to search for the service, check the actual Region and permissions, read any cost information, and only then create resources. Quick check: if your EC2 server appears missing, what simple console setting should you verify first? The selected AWS Region.

scenes.title: AWS shared responsibility model
scenes.narration: The central image divides a building into two halves. The blue AWS half represents security of the cloud. AWS secures the physical data centers, underlying servers, foundational networking, virtualization and managed infrastructure appropriate to the service. The orange customer half represents security in the cloud: what you build, store, configure and permit within your account. On the right are three groups of responsibilities. Data must be classified and protected. Applications and service configurations must be set safely. And identities and access permissions determine who may operate resources or see information. Identity tells the system who a person or workload is, while authorization decides what actions that identity can perform. Think of renting an office. The building owner maintains the structure, utilities and shared facilities, but the tenant controls office documents, staff access and internal procedures. This analogy helps, but AWS services differ in their responsibilities. With an EC2 virtual server, customers ordinarily maintain the guest operating system and installed application. With a more managed service, AWS may take on additional software tasks, but customers still decide who can access their information and how it is used. Now connect this to artificial intelligence. If a team uploads private student records to an AI application, AWS may protect infrastructure, but the team still needs a lawful data purpose, appropriate encryption, authorized users and safe handling rules. A misconfigured publicly accessible bucket is not fixed simply by AWS maintaining its data center securely. To decide responsibility, ask: is this the provider's underlying infrastructure, or is it my data, my application, my identity policy or a setting I control? Always confirm the exact division in the selected service's documentation.

scenes.title: Responsible use of AWS services
scenes.narration: Cloud resources are powerful, so using them responsibly matters just as much as using them correctly. The slide places an AWS shield in the center and connects it to four numbered duties. First, keep content and activity lawful and safe. Users should not misuse services for illegal acts or harmful content. Second, protect security. Do not attempt unauthorized access, interfere with other customers or bypass protections. Third, avoid network abuse, including activity that disrupts systems or degrades other users' service. Fourth, prevent messaging abuse such as unsolicited spam or deceptive phishing. Phishing means trying to trick people into disclosing information or clicking malicious links by pretending to be a trusted sender. As a practical example, a student building an AI email assistant should use consent-based test messages instead of sending thousands of unsolicited messages to strangers. An organization building a chatbot should apply identity and content safety controls rather than asking the model to produce harmful instructions. These principles are reflected in AWS's Acceptable Use Policy, often abbreviated AUP. The policy itself can change, so the current AWS publication is authoritative for exact wording and restrictions, not this diagram alone. The four corners are not four features to enable in a console; they are responsibilities to follow when designing and operating workloads. Safe cloud use also involves not sharing passwords, keeping access permissions narrow, and reviewing which data you upload to a model. Here is a comprehension question: could a test that floods someone else's website with requests be acceptable merely because it runs from your own AWS account? No. Ownership of a cloud account does not grant permission to disrupt another service. Always get proper authorization before running security or load tests.

scenes.title: Plan a safe learning budget
scenes.narration: This final slide is especially important for students experimenting with cloud AI services for the first time. The main message is that many services charge according to their pricing model and usage, so you should plan before you begin. Follow the arrows through four stages. First, use AI services carefully. You might call a text model, upload a file for analysis or run a virtual machine, and each activity may have different charges. Second, set a budget alert using the account's available billing and budgeting tools. A budget alert notifies you when actual or forecast spending crosses a chosen threshold. Look closely at the warning next to the bell: alerts do not automatically cap all spending. Charges can continue after a notification, and billing data may not appear instantaneously. Third, inspect charges regularly to understand which service and Region is creating cost. Fourth, clean up practice resources after an experiment. This may involve stopping or terminating an appropriate server, deleting temporary storage, removing an unused endpoint or switching off a provisioned service, depending on which resources you created. Merely closing the browser does not stop a running server. Imagine a college project where you launch a virtual computer to test an application. After the class, leaving it active for days may create unnecessary charges, even if nobody uses the project. For AI models, repeated inference requests, stored datasets and provisioned capacity can add costs. Set a modest experimental budget, check any eligibility for trial allowances without assuming everything is free, and review the current price details before deploying. If unexpected charges arise, investigate immediately and remove resources safely after preserving anything you need. Quick check: does creating a ten-dollar budget alert guarantee your bill cannot exceed ten dollars? No. The alert is a warning, not a universal spending cap. The lesson ends with a responsible habit: estimate, monitor, clean up and verify that resources have actually stopped billing.
